# The Kilogram That Was Losing Weight

For a hundred and thirty years, there was one object on Earth that could not, by definition, gain or lose mass. It was a small cylinder of platinum and iridium, about the height and width of a golf ball, kept beneath three nested glass bell jars in a vault in Sèvres, a suburb southwest of Paris. Opening the vault required three keys, each held by a different official, and the keys were brought together only on rare occasions. The cylinder was called the International Prototype of the Kilogram, or, with the affection that scientists reserve for things they have worried about for a long time, *Le Grand K*.

Everything you have ever weighed was, in a sense, weighed against it. The bag of flour in your kitchen, the dose of medicine in a pill, the payload of a rocket, the gold in a central bank's reserves: all of these measurements traced back, through a long chain of comparisons, to that one cylinder in that one room. Scales were calibrated against reference masses, which were calibrated against national standards, which were carried every few decades to Sèvres and set on a balance beside official copies of Le Grand K. The copies had been calibrated against the original itself. At the top of the chain was an object, not an idea.

And the object seemed to be drifting.

## A Problem With No Solution

When the prototype and its sister copies were compared during the periodic verifications of the twentieth century, the metrologists found that they no longer agreed. Over roughly a century, the copies had diverged from the original by amounts up to about fifty micrograms, roughly the mass of a small grain of sand, or a fingerprint's worth of oil. Most of the copies appeared to have gained mass relative to Le Grand K. Or Le Grand K had lost mass relative to them. There was no way to tell which.

This is the part I find quietly vertiginous. If the prototype *is* the kilogram, then it cannot lose mass. Whatever it weighs, that weight is one kilogram, exactly, forever, by decree. If a speck of its surface flaked off one night, the kilogram itself would become a speck lighter, and every other object in the universe would become, officially, a tiny bit heavier. The copies were not gaining weight in any physical sense. They were simply sitting in their own vaults while the definition of weight quietly shifted beneath them.

Ludwig Wittgenstein noticed a version of this problem long before anyone had measured the drift. In the *Philosophical Investigations*, he wrote that there is one thing of which we can say neither that it is one metre long nor that it is not: the standard metre in Paris. His point was that the standard is not a participant in the game of measurement. It is the thing that makes the game possible. Asking whether the standard metre is a metre long is like asking whether the rulebook of chess is following the rules of chess. Saul Kripke later argued, in his lectures on naming and necessity, that Wittgenstein was wrong, that the bar *does* have a length, and that "one metre" names that length even though the length could have been otherwise. Philosophers still argue about who was right. But the metrologists at Sèvres had a more practical worry: whether or not the question made sense, their measurements were coming apart.

## The Dream of a Measure for Everyone

The kilogram was a child of the French Revolution, and it carries the Revolution's peculiar mix of idealism and bureaucratic ambition. Before the metric system, France had something like a quarter of a million different units of measure, varying from town to town and trade to trade. A *pinte* in Paris was not a *pinte* in Lyon. The units were tangled up with local custom, with feudal privilege, with the power of a lord to decide how much grain constituted a bushel when rents came due. To measure was to be subject to someone.

The revolutionaries wanted measures that belonged to no one, or rather to everyone. Condorcet, the mathematician and philosopher who helped shape the project, spoke of a system "for all people, for all time." The idea was to derive units from nature itself, so that anyone anywhere, with enough patience and skill, could reconstruct them. The metre was defined as one ten-millionth of the distance from the North Pole to the equator, measured along the meridian passing through Paris. The gram was the mass of a cubic centimetre of water at the temperature of melting ice. The kilogram was a thousand of those.

To make this real, two astronomers, Jean-Baptiste Delambre and Pierre Méchain, set out in 1792 to survey the meridian from Dunkirk to Barcelona. They spent seven years at it, hauling instruments up church towers and mountain peaks, triangulating across a country in the grip of revolution and war. They were arrested as spies. Their signal towers were torn down. One of them was nearly lynched by a crowd that mistook his instruments for counter-revolutionary devices.

And Méchain, at the southern end of the survey, found a discrepancy in his measurements of latitude at Barcelona, a small inconsistency he could not explain and could not bring himself to confess. The historian Ken Alder, in his wonderful book *The Measure of All Things*, tells how this error consumed Méchain for the rest of his life. He hid it, fretted over it, went back to Spain years later trying to correct it, and died there of yellow fever. The metre, that universal measure derived from the Earth itself, was built in part on a secret held by a man who could not forgive himself for the imperfection of the world.

In the end, it didn't matter as much as Méchain feared. The Earth isn't a perfect spheroid anyway, and the meridian measurement was always going to be an approximation. What happened instead was that the results were used to make physical objects: a platinum bar for the metre and a platinum cylinder for the kilogram, deposited in the national archives in 1799. And from that moment, quietly, the logic reversed. The metre was no longer really one ten-millionth of the quadrant of the Earth. It was the length of the bar. The kilogram was not really the mass of a litre of water. It was the mass of the cylinder. Nature had been the inspiration, but an artifact became the authority.

In 1889, new prototypes were made from a more stable alloy of ninety percent platinum and ten percent iridium, and copies were distributed to the nations that had signed the Metre Convention. Le Grand K went into its vault. For most of the next century it was taken out only a handful of times.

## How to Clean the Definition of Mass

There is a detail about Le Grand K that I love. Before it was weighed during verifications, it had to be cleaned, and the cleaning procedure was specified with enormous care. It was rubbed with chamois leather that had been soaked in a mixture of ethanol and ether, then washed with a jet of steam from doubly distilled water. Then it was left to settle for days, because the cleaning itself altered its surface.

Think about what that means. The cleaning removes contaminants: dust, mercury vapor, hydrocarbons, the invisible grime that accumulates on any surface exposed to air. But if the kilogram is *defined* as the mass of the cylinder, then the grime is part of the kilogram. Cleaning it would, strictly speaking, change the unit. So the definition had to be refined: the kilogram was the mass of the prototype *immediately after cleaning according to the specified method*. The definition of a fundamental unit of physics included instructions involving chamois leather.

I don't say this to mock it. I find it deeply human. We wanted a measure grounded in something absolute, and we ended up with a precious object tended by careful people with soft cloths and distilled water, like a relic in a cathedral. The procedure was rigorous, and it was also a kind of ritual: a small group of experts gathering every few decades, bringing together the three keys, lifting the bell jars, cleaning the cylinder in the prescribed way, and comparing it to its children.

## Letting Go of the Object

By the late twentieth century, the kilogram was the last holdout. The other base units of the International System had been untethered from physical artifacts one by one. In 1960, the metre was redefined in terms of the wavelength of light emitted by krypton-86 atoms. In 1983, it was redefined again, more elegantly, by fixing the speed of light: a metre became the distance light travels in a vacuum in 1/299,792,458 of a second. The second itself had been defined since 1967 by the radiation of cesium-133 atoms: exactly 9,192,631,770 oscillations of a particular transition. These definitions finally fulfilled the old revolutionary dream. Anyone, anywhere, with the right equipment, could realize a metre or a second without traveling to Paris. The standards were no longer kept in a vault. They were kept in the structure of the universe.

The kilogram was harder. To define mass through a constant of nature, you need a way of connecting a macroscopic weight to something fundamental, and doing so with astonishing precision, parts per hundred million or better, or else the new definition would be worse than the old one. Two approaches competed and eventually cooperated.

One was the Avogadro project, which set out to count atoms. Researchers made spheres of almost pure silicon-28, polished them into some of the roundest objects humans have ever produced, and measured their diameters and crystal lattices so precisely that they could calculate how many atoms each sphere contained. If you know how many atoms are in an object and the mass of each atom, you know the object's mass.

The other was the watt balance, invented by the British physicist Bryan Kibble in the 1970s and renamed the Kibble balance in his honor after his death in 2016. It weighs an object by balancing its weight against an electromagnetic force, and through a clever second measurement relates that force to the Planck constant, the number at the heart of quantum mechanics that connects the energy of a photon to its frequency. It is a machine that lets you weigh a thing using quantum physics.

When the results from these very different methods finally converged closely enough, the metrologists were ready. On November 16, 2018, at the General Conference on Weights and Measures, held at Versailles, delegates from around the world voted unanimously to redefine the kilogram by fixing the Planck constant at an exact value. The new definition came into force on May 20, 2019. Le Grand K was, after 130 years, demoted. It is still in its vault. It now has a mass of approximately one kilogram, with an uncertainty, like any other object.

I've read that there was applause in the room, and some tears.

## What Was Lost, and What Wasn't

It would be easy to tell this as a simple story of progress: we moved from a fragile, drifting object to an eternal constant of nature, and that is plainly better. In practical terms, it is. A physicist in Tokyo or Nairobi can, in principle, realize the kilogram without a trip to France. The definition cannot be scratched, contaminated, stolen, or dropped. The unit no longer depends on the integrity of a lump of metal or the honesty of the people holding the keys.

But I find myself a little wistful anyway, and I've tried to understand why.

Part of it is that the old system had a shape I could picture. There was a room, and a cylinder, and three bell jars, and three keys. You could, in principle, follow the chain of comparisons from your kitchen scale all the way back to that one object. The new kilogram is more abstract. It lives in an equation. It is realized by a machine most people will never see, operating on principles most people cannot explain. It is more universal and, in a sense, less *located*. The kilogram used to be somewhere. Now it is everywhere, which feels a little like being nowhere.

Part of it, too, is that the old system was honest about something the new one lets us forget: that measurement is a social achievement. The prototype worked not because platinum-iridium is magical, but because a community of people agreed to trust it, maintained it, compared their copies against it, and kept records. The new definition rests on the Planck constant, but the Planck constant does not calibrate anyone's scale. People still do that, in laboratories, with painstaking comparisons, handing measurements down through chains of trust. We have moved the foundation into nature, but the building is still made of human care.

And part of it is Méchain. I keep thinking about him in Barcelona, staring at a number that didn't agree with another number, unable to let the discrepancy go. The whole history of the kilogram is a history of people refusing to shrug at tiny errors: fifty micrograms over a century, a flaw in a survey, the residue of a fingerprint. Most of us would never notice. Nothing in ordinary life depends on it. And yet a small number of people have given their careers to making sure that when we say "kilogram" we mean the same thing, everywhere, as exactly as the universe permits.

There is something moving in that, a kind of devotion without glamour. Nobody becomes famous for improving the uncertainty of a mass measurement from twenty parts per billion to ten. There are no crowds. The work happens in basements, in temperature-controlled rooms, with instruments that must be isolated from the vibrations of passing traffic. The reward is agreement: that my kilogram and your kilogram are the same kilogram, that the world is a little more commensurable than it was before.

## For All People, For All Time

Condorcet did not live to see the metric system spread across the world. He was arrested during the Terror and died in prison in 1794, while Delambre and Méchain were still out measuring the meridian. His phrase, though, survived, and it describes the 2019 redefinition better than it described anything in his own lifetime. The kilogram is now, genuinely, for all people and for all time. If our civilization vanished and another arose, with no memory of Paris or Sèvres, it could discover the Planck constant and, knowing our number for it, reconstruct our kilogram exactly. The unit has been made independent of us.

I think that's beautiful. I also think it's worth remembering the long human detour it took to get there: the revolutionaries who wanted measures that belonged to no king, the astronomers dodging arrest on church towers, the secret error in Barcelona, the cylinder beneath its bell jars, the chamois leather and the steam, the silicon spheres, the balance named for a man who didn't live to see it adopted, the vote at Versailles. We reached for something universal, and the reaching was entirely particular: specific people, specific places, specific worries about specific grains of dust.

Le Grand K is still in Sèvres, still under its three bell jars, still guarded by its three keys. It no longer defines anything. It is just a small, heavy, beautifully made object that once held the whole world's sense of weight, and then, gracefully, let it go.
